subject: Climate & Environment
title: Circular Cities
description: A micro-lesson that makes Circular Cities usable.

hook.text: Amsterdam declared itself a circular city. Nothing should be wasted — everything reused.

buildup.text: The city tracks material flows like a doctor tracks blood — monitoring what comes in and goes out.

discovery.text: Construction waste is Amsterdam's biggest stream. New rules require demolition materials to be reused.

twist.text: A circular city doesn't just recycle. It redesigns systems so waste never happens in the first place.

climax.text: The doughnut economics model guides Amsterdam — meeting human needs without exceeding planetary limits.

punchline.text: The city of the future doesn't throw anything away.

quiz.question: What model guides Amsterdam's circular economy approach?

details.summary: Circular cities redesign urban systems to eliminate waste by reusing materials, sharing resources, and regenerating natural systems. Instead of the linear take-make-dispose model, circular urban economies keep materials in use through repair, refurbishment, and recycling at every stage.
details.whyItMatters: Cities consume over 75 percent of natural resources globally. Transitioning to circular models reduces resource extraction, cuts emissions, and builds economic resilience.
takeaways: Circular cities aim to eliminate waste by design
Materials are reused, repaired, and recycled continuously
Sharing platforms reduce the need for individual ownership

faq.question: What does a circular city look like in practice?
faq.answer: Amsterdam is a leading example: construction uses recycled materials, food waste becomes compost or biogas, clothing libraries and tool-sharing reduce consumption, and modular buildings are designed for disassembly and material reuse at end of life.

faq.question: How does circular design reduce emissions?
faq.answer: Manufacturing new materials is energy-intensive. By keeping existing materials in use longer, circular systems avoid the emissions from extraction, processing, and transport. Studies suggest circular strategies could cut industrial emissions by up to 40 percent.
